input:
In this study, two different membranes are compared for the separation of ethanol and water by pervaporation. Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane out as a vapour. The feed used in the experiments consisted of 85 wt% ethanol in water, and the tests were carried out at 60 °C. Only this single feed composition was investigated, and none of the tests was run for longer than 500 h.

Two quantities are used to describe the performance of the membranes. The flux is the mass of material that permeates through a unit area of membrane in one hour, expressed in kg m-2 h-1, and the separation factor is the ratio of water to alcohol in the permeate divided by the corresponding ratio in the feed, and is therefore dimensionless. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 2.3 kg m-2 h-1 together with a separation factor of 120, although its flux fell by 13% over the course of 500 h. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, achieved a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a much higher separation factor of 560, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h to within the error of the measurements.

Overall, the results show a familiar trade-off: the polymer membrane offers the higher throughput, while the zeolite membrane offers the better selectivity and the more stable performance. It is worth remarking that flux, selectivity and stability are rarely all reported together for one and the same membrane, which is part of what makes this comparison useful, although the findings are limited to the single composition and the durations that were actually tested.
target:
Two membranes were compared for the pervaporation of a feed of 85 wt% ethanol in water at 60 °C. Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. The polymer membrane gave the higher flux and the lower separation factor; the zeolite membrane gave the lower flux, the higher separation factor, and the stable flux. The comparison was made on one feed, over a bounded duration, so that flux, selectivity and stability rest on the same run for each membrane.

Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 120, and its flux fell 13% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 560, with its flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error.

The comparison is a trade between rate and selectivity, with stability standing on the zeolite side. One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the standing of either membrane outside the tested composition and duration is not established by these results. Within those bounds, the choice between the membranes is a choice of what the separation is for.
